I have been tinkering with sourdough for almost two years now and it still feels like I learn something new every batch. The house smells incredible on baking days and the kids always hover around the oven waiting for the first slice. My current starter lives in a plain wide-mouth mason jar on the kitchen counter. I named him Gerald because the first time he doubled in size he looked like a little old man with a bubbly white beard.

Gerald gets fed on a 1:5:5 ratio most days. That means 20 grams of starter, 100 grams of filtered water, and 100 grams of a 50/50 mix of bread flour and whole wheat. I stir it with a chopstick until it looks like thick pancake batter, then pop a rubber band around the jar to track rise. In summer the kitchen stays around 78F so bulk fermentation usually takes about five hours from the time I mix the dough. In winter I sometimes move the bowl near the fridge vent or use the proofing setting on the oven to keep the temperature steady.

The basic loaf I make most often is a simple country sourdough. I mix 350 grams of water, 100 grams of active starter, 500 grams of bread flour, and 10 grams of salt. After a quick mix I let it rest for thirty minutes before doing four sets of stretch-and-folds every thirty minutes. Once the dough feels smooth and has a bit of spring I shape it into a boule and let it proof in a banneton lined with a floured tea towel. When it passes the poke test I slash it with a lame and slide it into a preheated Dutch oven.

Baking schedule is always the same: 500F covered for 20 minutes, then drop the temperature to 450F, uncover, and bake another 25 minutes. The crust comes out deep mahogany with nice ear development when everything aligns. I let the loaf cool on a wire rack for at least two hours before slicing. Cutting too early always leads to gummy crumb and sad faces at breakfast.

### Troubleshooting

- **Dense crumb**: Usually means the bulk ferment was too short or the starter was not quite active enough. I have started taking the temperature of the dough now instead of just guessing.
- **Flat loaf**: Overproofing is the most common culprit. If the dough feels overly airy and collapses when I try to shape it I know I waited too long.
- **Sour taste is too strong**: Gerald can get very tangy if I forget a feeding. I sometimes give him a 1:10:10 refresh the night before baking to calm him down.
- **Crust too pale**: The oven might not have been fully preheated or I need to bake five minutes longer uncovered. I also experimented with adding a few ice cubes to the Dutch oven for extra steam but that sometimes makes the bottom soggy.
- **Starter not rising**: If Gerald looks sluggish I discard most of him and feed twice a day for a couple of days. He usually perks right back up.

I keep a small notebook next to the flour bin where I jot down exact times, temperatures, and hydration percentages. Some batches turn out better than others but even the failures make pretty good toast. My next experiment is trying to incorporate a little rye into the starter to see if it changes the flavor profile.
